titel: Chart patterns and the state of research
kurz: How the head and shoulders, double top, triangle, flag and cup are constructed, and how much of this can also be found in pure noise.

bloecke.md:
A chart pattern is a claim made up of three parts. From a certain point, the price moves in a particular direction, it runs as far as a target, and below a defined level the claim is considered refuted. Only the third part distinguishes a pattern from a mere story. Trading a pattern without a defined invalidation point means trading on a mood instead of a pattern.

The textbook forms can be divided into two groups. Reversal patterns such as the head and shoulders and the double top are supposed to signal the end of a trend. Continuation patterns such as the triangle, the flag and the cup with handle are supposed to signal a pause in an existing trend. Both groups derive their price target in the same way. The height of the pattern is projected from the breakout point in the direction of the breakout. This target rule is a convention without any theoretical justification. It has appeared in the literature since the 1930s, without anyone ever deriving why the height of the pattern, of all things, should be the right yardstick.

bloecke.titel: Five patterns and where they are vague
zeilen: Head and shoulders
Three highs, the middle one the highest; neckline through the two intermediate lows
Downward trend reversal as soon as the neckline breaks
How far the shoulders may differ from each other; no textbook gives a figure for this
Double top
Two highs at a similar level with a low in between
Reversal; the target is the height of the highs above the intermediate low, projected downwards
What ‘similar’ means, for example a gap of 1%, 3% or 5%
Triangle
Falling highs and rising lows (symmetrical) or one horizontal edge
Continuation in the direction of the breakout; the target is the width of the base
The direction, which is only known after the breakout and therefore after the fact
Flag
Short countertrend consolidation after a steep rise (flagpole)
Continuation; the target is the length of the pole, measured from the breakout
How steep ‘steep’ is and how short ‘short’ is
Cup with handle
Rounded bottom over weeks, followed by a small pullback
Breakout above the rim of the cup; the target is the depth of the cup
The rounding itself, which emerges when the chart is traced afterwards and not when it is watched in real time

bloecke.md:
## Patterns in random series

An important test can be carried out at no cost. You generate a price series that, by its construction, contains no information whatsoever. Each step is an independent random draw, and the next value is related to the previous one only in that it starts from it. Such a random walk cannot contain any patterns in the sense of predictability; every shape in it is noise by definition. Then you look at the series.

The following series was generated in this way. It has 80 steps and a starting value of 100, and each step return is normally distributed with a mean of zero and a standard deviation of 1.2%. This corresponds to just under 19% annual volatility and is therefore within the realistic range of a stock index. It was generated with the Mersenne Twister generator and seed 32. The series is therefore reproducible and not drawn by hand.

bloecke.titel: Head-and-shoulders pattern in a random path
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation: random walk with 80 steps, normally distributed step returns (mean 0, standard deviation 1.2%), starting value 100 and random number generator seed 32. By its construction, the curve contains no usable information.

bloecke.md:
The pattern meets all the textbook criteria: three highs with the highest in the middle, two shoulders at approximately the same height, a slightly falling neckline through the intermediate lows and even an almost symmetrical time axis (25 steps from the left shoulder to the head, 26 from the head to the right shoulder). The signal also worked. After the neckline broke at step 65, the series fell from 99.75 to 94.24, that is, by around 5.5% in fifteen steps. The calculated price target of about 91 (head minus neckline, projected from the break point) was not reached by the end of the series.

The fact that the signal worked has no significance, because in a series without information a signal can only be right by chance. Nor is the series a rare lucky find. If you mechanically check a thousand independently generated random paths of this length for such a figure, you find it in around 158 out of 1,000 cases, that is, in roughly every sixth pure random path. A head and shoulders is defined here as three local highs whose middle one is at least 3% above both outer ones, whose outer ones are at most 3% apart and whose intermediate lows differ from each other by at most 4%.

On a finished historical chart, every pattern looks obvious. Behind this is hindsight bias, which Fischhoff described experimentally in 1975. What has happened appears predictable in retrospect. In an honest test, you cover the right-hand part of the chart and record, candle by candle, what you would do at each point in time, with entry, stop and target. Most patterns disappear in the process, because only in retrospect is it decided which high was the right shoulder and which was merely an intermediate high. A pattern that can only be reliably identified in retrospect describes the past price movement and provides no signal.

## Empirical studies on patterns

The scientific study of patterns has a fundamental methodological problem. As long as patterns are identified by eye, they cannot be tested, because two examiners count different cases. As early as 1995, Osler and Chang searched for the head-and-shoulders pattern in exchange rates using an objective, computer-based method. In 2000, Lo, Mamaysky and Wang used an algorithmic definition for ten patterns. The price series is smoothed, local extrema are determined formally, and the patterns result from their sequence. For US equities from 1962 to 1996, they found that several patterns provide additional information, in a statistical sense, compared with the unconditional distribution of returns. The finding goes no further than that, because additional information does not yet mean a tradable profit after costs.

The pattern that was subsequently the focus of further research is the head and shoulders. In 2007, Savin, Weller and Zvingelis found risk-adjusted excess returns of 5% to 7% a year in the S&P 500 and the Russell 2000 for the years 1990 to 1999. However, this only applied when the pattern signal was added to the market portfolio. For a stand-alone trading strategy, the authors explicitly found little evidence. This is probably the most favourable finding that exists on chart patterns, and it comes from a single decade in a single market.

bloecke.titel: Results of 95 modern studies on technical analysis
bloecke.unter: In their review, Park and Irwin (2007) count how the results turn out, and they note themselves that most of these studies have methodological flaws such as data snooping, rule selection after the fact and cost assumptions that are too low.

bloecke.md: The 56 positive findings explain why both camps can cite studies. The picture changes once the multiple testing problem is taken seriously. In 1992, Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron found strong evidence for simple moving average and breakout rules using Dow data from 1897 to 1986. In 1999, Sullivan, Timmermann and White tested the same family of rules by bootstrap across the entire universe of possible rules. For 1897 to 1986, the results withstood the correction for data snooping, but in the ten years that followed (1987 to 1996), even the best rule no longer delivered a significant advantage. In 2012, Bajgrowicz and Scaillet, using false discovery methods, likewise found no persistence for 1897 to 2011. The rules that later turned out best could not be selected in advance, and even low trading costs wiped out the advantage within the sample as well. With enough variants tested, you will inevitably find a good one, even in pure noise. Harvey, Liu and Zhu therefore call for a t-statistic above 3.0 for new signals instead of the usual 2.0.

An algorithmic definition has to specify three things that a person glosses over when looking at a chart: how strongly the series is smoothed before highs and lows are counted; how many steps an extremum must be from its neighbours to count as a high in its own right; and which percentage tolerances are permitted between shoulders and intermediate lows.

Each of these three settings changes the number of hits considerably. If you loosen the shoulder tolerance from 3% to 6%, the number of patterns found rises markedly, and with it the number of cases in the random path. This is where a testable statement parts company with an untestable one. If you set the tolerances only after looking at the results, you are searching for a pattern instead of testing it.

## Win rate and expected value

In courses and books, patterns are advertised with win rates such as 63%, 71% or 84%. Such figures are meaningless without three additional pieces of information: how large the gain is on a win, how large the loss is on a failure and what the turnover costs. The result is determined by the expected value per trade and not by the proportion of winners.

bloecke.formel: E = p × G - (1 - p) × V - K
bloecke.erklaerung: E is the expected value per trade in euros after costs. A pattern only contributes something if E is positive. The costs K comprise the order fee for buying and selling, half the spread on each side and the slippage. A common assumption is 0.10% of the position volume per round turn.
variablen: average gain per win in euros
average loss per failure in euros
total cost of the round turn in euros
bloecke.beispiel: Position €5,000, profit target +3.0% (€150), stop -1.5% (€75), costs 0.10% (€5). E = 0 holds when p × 150 - (1 - p) × 75 = 5, that is, at p = 80/225 = 35.6%. Without costs, the threshold would be 33.3%.

bloecke.md:
The table assumes a gain of €150 per win, a loss of €75 per failure, costs of 0.10% per round turn and tax of 26.375%. The tax rate is made up of 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act) plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge under Section 4 SolzG 1995 (Solidarity Surcharge Act). Church tax is not taken into account, and the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG) is assumed to have already been used up elsewhere. The order fees reduce the capital gain directly, because they can be allocated to the individual transaction (Section 20(4) sentence 1 EStG). Seminar fees, charting software and data feeds, by contrast, do not reduce it, because the deduction of income-related expenses (Werbungskosten) is excluded under the flat-rate withholding tax.

Twenty percentage points of win rate separate the worst row from the best. Five percentage points separate the last row with a loss from the first row with a profit. No pattern study measures win rates with this precision, and no advertising claim states the associated ratio of gains to losses.

Gains are taxed in the year in which they arise; losses are only offset. Losses on shares go into the separate share loss pot (Aktien-Verlusttopf) and may only be offset against gains from share sales (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG). All other losses go into the general loss pot. Unused losses are carried forward indefinitely but earn no interest. With high turnover, the tax for good years is due immediately, while losses from bad years can only be offset later.

## Trading frequency and costs

A pattern signal is only worth something if it earns more than the cost of the turnover it generates. This hurdle is high, because costs grow linearly with trading frequency, but the claimed advantage does not.

bloecke.titel: Annual cost burden by trading frequency
bloecke.unter: Calculated with total costs of 0.10% per round turn (fee, half spread, slippage) on the position volume. The reference line marks the most favourable documented pattern finding of 5% to 7% a year, risk-adjusted and only as an additional signal (Savin, Weller, Zvingelis 2007).

serien.name: Cost burden in percentage points p.a.

bloecke.md: At around 60 round turns a year, that is, just over one a week, trading costs already eat up the whole of the most favourable pattern advantage ever measured, and that is before tax. Trading flags on an hourly chart can easily add up to several hundred round turns. A pattern would then have to deliver double-digit percentage points a year just to end up at zero after costs. An advantage of this order of magnitude is not documented anywhere in the published literature on patterns.

schritte.titel: Write the rule before looking at the data
schritte.text: Define in writing the pattern, the percentage tolerances, entry, stop, target and time limit, and do so completely enough that another person would find the same cases.
Determine the securities, the interval and the period. Without this, the selection is made after the fact on the basis of the result.

schritte.titel: Collect at least a hundred cases
schritte.text: With twenty cases, a win rate of 60% cannot be statistically distinguished from 50%. With fewer than a hundred cases, no conclusion is possible.
Apply the same rule to generated random paths with the same volatility. If it hits just as often there, its success is based on the geometry of random price movements and not on a pattern.
Assume costs of 0.10% per round turn and tax of 26.375% on the net profit. Only what is left after that counts as the result; figures before costs and taxes are advertising claims.

bloecke.md: Chart patterns are geometric descriptions of past price movements. Their interpretations can partly be measured. However, the measured effects are small, methodologically fragile and so far nowhere large enough to offset turnover costs and flat-rate withholding tax. A tested rule is distinguished from a narrated figure by the record of its test; the difference cannot be seen on the chart itself.

mitnehmen: A pattern only becomes a statement once entry, target and invalidation point are fixed before the trade.
Around 158 out of 1,000 pure random paths contain a head-and-shoulders pattern according to formal criteria, so the appearance of a figure proves nothing.
The most favourable documented finding is 5% to 7% a year, risk-adjusted; it applies only to an addition to the market portfolio and comes from a single decade.
Win rates without the ratio of gains to losses and without costs mean nothing; in the illustrative calculation, five percentage points of win rate decide between profit and loss.
With costs of 0.10% per round turn, trading costs exceed the entire pattern advantage ever measured once you reach around 60 round turns a year.

begriffe.text: Line connecting the two intermediate lows of a head-and-shoulders pattern. In chart analysis, a break of this line is regarded as the trigger signal. The calculated price target is the height of the head above the neckline, projected from the break point.

Price series whose individual steps are drawn independently of each other. By its construction it contains no predictability and serves as a null model. Anything that occurs in it just as often as in real prices is not a pattern.
Bias caused by multiple testing. If many rules or parameters are tested on the same data, it is highly likely that one will appear successful, even if none of them has a real advantage.
Share of winning trades at which the expected value per trade is zero. Without costs, p = 1/(1 + reward-to-risk ratio). Fees, spread and slippage raise this threshold noticeably.

Separate offsetting pool kept by the bank under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG. Losses from share sales may only be offset against gains from share sales, not against interest, fund gains or gains from derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte).
